terms.context: Individual accelerators fail rarely, but scaling to thousands of nodes multiplies component failure rates until interruption becomes a continuous operating condition. At cluster scale, Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) drops from years to hours, turning failure recovery into a core execution path. This appendix collects the quantitative reliability calculations behind the book's fault-tolerance chapters, deriving failure probabilities, Young-Daly optimal checkpoint intervals, and availability stacking models. In C³ terms, it develops the coordination axis, where checkpointing, recovery, and availability determine how much of the fleet's compute and communication becomes useful work.

Reliability engineers characterize components using two complementary metrics. The **Failure in Time (FIT)** rate counts failures per $10^9$ device-hours of operation---a unit chosen because individual components fail so rarely that failures-per-hour would produce inconveniently small numbers. This is the **MTBF Cascade**\index{MTBF Cascade}: reliability degrades linearly with component count at each level, and the levels compound. A node with `{python} ReliabilityStringsMtbfRecap.node_mtbf_hours_str` MTBF sounds reliable. A cluster of `{python} ReliabilityStringsMtbfRecap.nodes_10k_str` such nodes has an MTBF of just `{python} ReliabilityStringsMtbfRecap.cluster_mtbf_10k_hours_str`---a failure every few hours is the expected steady state.

## Silent Data Corruption (SDC) Attention Perturbation Model {#sec-appdx-reliability-sdc-perturbation}

terms.canonical_expansion: single-bit errors or arithmetic logic unit
terms.context: Not all hardware faults manifest as explicit system crashes, ECC double-bit errors, or kernel traps. **Silent Data Corruption (SDC)** occurs when single-bit errors or arithmetic logic unit (ALU) faults slip past parity checks, corrupting tensor values in SRAM, HBM, or register files without triggering an exception. In deep learning workloads, SDC is particularly dangerous because single corrupted floating-point values propagate through non-linear operations, destabilizing fleet-wide training [@dixit2021silent].

Consider an IEEE 754 half-precision floating-point (FP16) tensor element representing a query vector $Q_{i,k}$, activation value, or weight matrix entry. FP16 allocates 16 total bits: 1 sign bit ($s$), 5 exponent bits ($e$), and 10 mantissa bits ($m$).
